ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: The broad, long tongue-mark is a Buddha-mark that Chan records transfer to mountains, trees, snow, letters, and responsive speech when these are made to voice the teaching.
EvidenceBody: Dahui Zonggao says that even if all grasses and trees displayed broad, long tongues and spoke until the end of time, they would still deliver only half the canon. Hongzhi Zhengjue instead says wind-blown trees and snowy ground expose the tongue-mark with nowhere to hide it.

Feiyin Tongrong gives every manifested body such a tongue to speak, then asks what it says. Nanyuan Daoming answers a request for one word by sticking out his tongue and postponing speech until he has the mark. The image can therefore magnify speech, relocate it into the whole scene, or expose the inadequacy of speech.

DraftEvidence.ZenBend: A Buddha's bodily sign becomes an encounter instrument for asking what truly speaks: the entire landscape may display it, yet immeasurable speech can still be judged only half the matter.
DraftEvidence.CounterexampleOrLimit: The corpus does not treat every sound as a complete teaching or make physical tongue length the point. Dahui explicitly limits even universal, endless speech.

ComparedThings: landscape and speech deployments of that mark
DifferentThingTest.Reason: The latter deliberately transfers the same bodily sign; it does not create another referent.

DraftEvidence.AliasRationale: The forms retain the bodily mark and its recurrent speaking construction.

ModifierControls.Finding: The headword is the broad-long tongue mark, not generic eloquence.

FamilyControls.Finding: The ordinary tongue and speaking-capacity term has broader uses.
Non-sentient things speaking is a related case family.
Dahui's half-canon judgement limits the tongue-mark's speech.
